attribution.note: Marcus's own words in a footnote to his signed post.

semantics.note: Unhedged present-tense generalization about LLMs. The normalisation keeps its meaning and scope.

contract.note: The plain reading (LLMs do not reliably recognize when they lack knowledge, measured by calibration and abstention) is the ordinary meaning of the idiom. The absolute 'zero self-knowledge' reading would fare worse, so the interpretation matters. The Apr–Jun 2025 window is reasonable.

evidence.note: AbstentionBench, posted June 10, 2025 (inside the window): 20 frontier models on 20 datasets. It finds abstention unsolved, scaling of little help, and only partial gains from prompting.

May 2025 study of 80 models on MMLU-Pro. Calibration varies, some models estimate uncertainty well, and results are task-sensitive. This qualifies an absolute reading but does not show reliability across tasks.
Anthropic research from 2022 (company disclosure) on an earlier model generation, outside the window. It shows partial self-knowledge that generalizes imperfectly.

reviews.rationale: Under the fair plain reading, a primary multi-model evaluation from inside the window (e1) shows widespread failure to abstain on unanswerable or underspecified questions. e2 and e3 show that some uncertainty signals exist in bounded settings, but not reliable recognition across varied tasks. The contradiction condition is not met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post, not a quote of the sources he cites.

semantics.note: Universal, unhedged present-tense claim. 'Current LLM system' fairly renders 'the systems' in context.

contract.note: Context supports reading 'trusted' as trusted to respect safety constraints in autonomous roles. The speaker gave no threshold for 'trusted' and no defined population, so the evaluator's choices on both determine scoring.

evidence.note: October 2025 paper on the June study of 16 selected models. Misbehavior appeared from every developer in some cases. It does not show violations by every relevant system or define a trust standard.

reviews.rationale: The only evidence covers selected models, with misbehavior found at the developer level. It does not show that each relevant system fails, and nothing shows any system adhering dependably. The universal claim is neither established nor refuted by the packet.

semantics.note: The 'might do better' clause stays hedged and is not scored. The scored part is the firm claim that confabulation remains widespread. 'Even' is slightly loose wording but harmless.

contract.note: Reading 'widespread' as a recurring problem across multiple model families, not as most responses being false, is ordinary and fair. The contract also correctly treats the 'might' clause as unscored.

evidence.note: OpenAI system card, April 2025 (company disclosure). o3 hallucination rates were 51% on SimpleQA and 33% on PersonQA, and other models were also nonzero. These results are not shown to be with browsing enabled.
Independent Phare benchmark, May 2025. It finds fabricated details across leading models from eight labs, with variation by prompt and by model.

reviews.rationale: Two evaluations from inside the window, one an independent multi-lab benchmark and one OpenAI's own figures for o3, show recurring fabrication across model families, including o3. Variation between models does not reach the contradiction condition (confabulation confined to isolated cases). The hedged clause about improvement is not scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in the post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'people', 'few' and the 'when' framing. This is a present-tense observation about funding appetite.

contract.note: Narrowing 'people' to funders or investors, and reading 'few' as scarce relative to LLMs, is an ordinary reading, though the speaker supplied neither. The undefined denominator and architecture class leave the result dependent on interpretation.

evidence.note: June 10, 2025 investor disclosure (company disclosure) showing backing for a logic-based AI firm. It is one exception, with no denominator and no evidence that the firm targets instruction-following.
OpenAI's $40B round in March 2025, before the window. It shows heavy LLM funding but provides no comparison with alternative architectures.

reviews.rationale: The packet has only individual announcements: one alternative-AI investment and one LLM mega-round outside the window. No representative dataset or denominator shows whether interest in controllable alternatives was scarce or broad, so neither condition is met.
